ety.text: Inherited from Middle English ake, hok, oek, ok, oke, from Old English aac, āc, ǣċ, from Proto-West Germanic *aik, from Proto-Germanic *aiks (“oak”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂eyǵ- (“oak”). Cognates From Proto-Germanic: Scots aik, ake, yik (“oak”), North Frisian iake, iik (“oak”), Saterland Frisian Eeke (“oak”), West Frisian iik (“oak”), Cimbrian aicha, oach (“oak”), Dutch eik (“oak”), German Eiche (“oak”), Luxembourgish Eech (“oak”), Vilamovian aach, aeh́, ǡh́ (“oak”), Danish eg (“oak”), Faroese, Icelandic, and Norwegian Nynorsk eik (“oak”), Norwegian Bokmål eik, ek (“oak”), Swedish ek (“oa…

senses.d: A deciduous tree with distinctive deeply lobed leaves, acorns, and notably strong wood, typically of England and northeastern North America, included in genus Quercus.
A rich brown color, like that of oak wood.
Any member of species of the genus Quercus, in family Fagaceae.
she-oaks in Allocasuarina and Casuarina, of family Casuarinaceae
white oaks Lagunaria, in family Malvaceae
poison oak Toxicodendron, in family Anacardiaceae
tanbark oaks or stone oaks, of species of genera Lithocarpus and Notholithocarpus in family Fagaceae.
Having a rich brown color, like that of oak wood.
Made of oak wood or timber.
ex: an oak table, oak beam, etc.

senses.d: To expose to oak in order for the oak to impart its flavors.

grp.label: tree or shrub of the genus Quercus

ety.text: Inherited from Middle French chesne, from Old French chesne, chaisne, chasne, from Vulgar Latin *cassanus (attested in Medieval Latin as casnus), probably from Gaulish kassanos. Some Old French forms possibly influenced by fraisne, fresne (cf. modern frêne). Compare Occitan casse, Franco-Provençal châno.
From Latin rōbur (“hard oak”, “hardness”), from ruber (“red”) (for its reddish hardwood), from Proto-Indo-European *h₁rudʰrós, from the root *h₁rewdʰ- (“red”). Cognate with Sicilian rùvulu.

es:roble.gl: oak, several species of the genus Quercus.

ety.text: From former robre, from Latin rōbore, singular ablative of rōbur (“a kind of hard oak”), whence also Aragonese robre (“oak”) and Catalan roure (“oak”).

From Old Galician-Portuguese carvalho of uncertain origin. Possibly from a local Latin *carbālius via Paleo-Hispanic, perhaps ultimately of Iberian origin. Cognate to Asturian carbayu, carba, Galician carballo, carba, and Spanish carvajo.
From Latin quercea, nominalized feminine form of the adjective querceus (“oaken, of oak”), derived from quercus (“oak”). Compare Neapolitan and Sicilian cerza.
From Late Latin farnea, feminine form of farneus.

es:encina.gl: holm oak, live oak, evergreen oak

ety.text: Inherited from Old Spanish enzina, from Vulgar Latin ilicīna, based on Latin īlex (“holm oak”). Compare Asturian ardina or Catalan alzina (“holm oak”).

es:carrasca.gl: any of various plants, especially the holm oak (Quercus ilex)

ety.text: From the root *karr-, of Pre-Roman origin.
